title: Parse key=value Settings
oneLiner: Read settings text line by line into a dictionary, skipping comments, blank lines and malformed lines, and splitting only at the first equals sign.
keyTakeaway: Parse text defensively, one line at a time: trim, skip what you don't understand, split at the first separator only (Split('=', 2) / partition), trim both halves, and let later lines override earlier ones. Windows line endings leave a \r behind unless you trim.
explanation:
Write ParseSettings(text), which reads lines of key=value settings into a dictionary of strings. The rules: lines are separated by \n; trim spaces from each line, and skip it if it's empty or starts with #; split it at the first = only, so values can contain =; trim the key and the value; skip lines with no = or with an empty key; and if a key appears twice, the later value wins. An empty value is allowed. "host = plc-1\nport=502" gives {"host": "plc-1", "port": "502"}.

In C#, line.Split('=', 2) splits into at most 2 parts, and line.IndexOf('=') finds the first one if you'd rather use Substring. In Python, key, sep, value = line.partition("=") splits at the first = and leaves sep empty when there isn't one. Trim with Trim() / strip().

One test uses Windows line endings, \r\n. Splitting on \n leaves a \r at the end of each line, which trimming removes; that's a common real-world surprise when files move between Windows and Linux. Settings files usually come from disk (File.ReadAllText, Path.read_text), but the exercise passes the text in directly: the parsing code is the same.

visualizationSteps.message: Six lines: "# comment", an empty line, "mode = auto", "bad line", "url = http://x/?a=b" and "mode=manual".
Line 1 is a comment and line 2 is blank: skip both.
Line 3: split at the first =, trim both sides: key "mode", value "auto".
Line 4 has no = at all: skip it rather than crash.
Line 5: only the first = splits, so the value keeps its own =.
Line 6 sets mode again: the later value replaces the earlier one.

complexity.note: Splitting, trimming and splitting each line again touch each of the n characters a constant number of times; the lines and the dictionary hold O(n) characters.
